title: Apparent Temperature Explorer
creator: Hank R. & Claude Code
subject: Environmental Monitoring
description: Wind chill and heat index drawn as two regimes of one apparent-temperature surface, with a target selector that shows objects cooling to the air temperature and a wet bulb zone where evaporative cooling fails.

learningObjectives: Calculate apparent temperature from air temperature, wind speed and humidity.
Explain why wind dominates in cold conditions and humidity dominates in hot ones.
State that wind chill is a rate of heat loss from a warm body, not a temperature the air reaches.
Identify the wet bulb limit beyond which evaporative cooling cannot work.
prerequisites: Chapter 8: relative humidity and wet bulb temperature
Chapter 10: wind chill, heat index and the wind speed unit table

keyQuestions: Why does the same wind speed matter enormously at minus 20 degrees and not at all at 20 degrees?
Does a car parked in a freezing wind get colder than the air around it?
Why is 45 degrees in the Sahara easier to survive than 33 degrees on the Gulf Coast?
What is physically happening when the wet bulb temperature passes 35 degrees?
commonMisconceptions: Wind chill is a temperature the air actually reaches.
Pipes and cars freeze at the wind chill value rather than the air temperature.
Hotter air is always more dangerous than cooler air.
Wind chill and heat index are unrelated ideas that happen to share a name.
assessmentOpportunities: Reads an apparent temperature and its difference from the actual reading for a given condition.
Explains the object-versus-body distinction in their own words.
Uses the cross-section view to describe the diminishing return of extra wind speed.
